food.text: By the 17th century, coffee had surpassed the global spice trade in importance. Up until the end of that century, Yemen was the world's main coffee producer, and its port of Mocha was the world's largest shipping port for coffee.

By the early 16th century, coffee drinking had spread from Yemen to Mecca, and on to Cairo, Damascus and Istanbul. It soon became a central part of urban social life, despite debates in Muslim society over whether it was permissible.

Al-Ahsa came under Ottoman rule in 1550. The oasis was one of the few places on the Arabian Peninsula where rice was grown, and its more than 280 artesian springs allowed year-round farming among more than 2.5 million palm trees.
In the late 16th century, Yemen developed a booming coffee economy. Farmers grew coffee on mountain terraces above the Tihamah plain, and trade routes linked Yemen's ports to Jeddah and Cairo.

In 1511, conservative imams at a theological court in Mecca banned coffee for its stimulating effects. The ban was overturned in 1524 by an order of Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I, after Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issued a fatwa allowing coffee consumption.

Mokha, a port on Yemen's Red Sea coast, was the major marketplace for coffee from the 16th through the 19th century. The coffee itself did not grow in Mokha but was transported there from Ethiopia and inland Yemen before being shipped abroad.

Before the Ottomans arrived in 1538, Mokha was just a small fishing village. The Ottomans built it into the first port north of the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, and by the first quarter of the 18th century it had reached its peak as a coffee-trading port.

Sailing the Red Sea in 1625, Portuguese Jesuit missionary Jerónimo Lobo reported that Ottoman law required every ship entering the Red Sea to put in at Mokha and pay duty on its cargo. This rule helped make Mokha the major city of Ottoman-controlled Arabia, even though its Pasha lived two days' journey inland in Sana'a.

By the early 18th century, English, Dutch and French companies maintained trading posts at Mokha, keeping it a major coffee-exporting port until the early 19th century. Passing through in 1752 and 1756, traveler Remedius Prutky counted ten European ships anchored there: three French, four English, two Dutch and one Portuguese.

Arabia's ancient frankincense trade had long since faded by the medieval period. Centuries later, coffee brought Yemen back into international commerce, flowing out through the Red Sea port of al-Mocha.

In the 18th century, a plague killed half of Mokha's population, and the town never really recovered. By the 1830s, its coffee trade had been overtaken by Ethiopia, which sold the same type of coffee for a third of the price of Arabia's.

The Yemeni port of Mokha was so well known for its coffee trade from the 15th to 17th century that Europeans began calling coffee imports from Arabia 'Mochas.' This happened even though coffee from Yemen itself was uncommon and often mixed with beans from Abyssinia.

art.text: In 1504, Amir ibn Abd Al-Wahhab of the Tahirid dynasty commissioned the Amiriya Madrasa in Rada, Yemen, an example of Tahirid architecture. The building served three roles at once, as a mosque, a madrasa, and Wahhab's own private residence.

The present town of Shibam in Yemen dates to 1533, standing on a site inhabited for about 1,700 years. Its houses are built of mudbrick, with about 500 tower blocks rising five to eleven stories high.

Within the courtyard of the Great Mosque of Sanaa stands a domed structure dating to the 16th century, an Ottoman building that resembles the Ka'ba in Mecca. It was built using an ablaq technique of alternating layers of colored materials.

The Al-Mahdi Mosque, also called the Mosque of the Dome of the Mahdi, was built in Sanaa in 1651 by order of Imam Mahdi Abbas bin Mansour. It stands in the Al-Kareem Al-Mahdi neighborhood of the city's historic western Sarar district.

Wahhab funded the Amiriya Madrasa with wealth he had amassed through trade across the Indian Ocean from the port city of Aden. As Sultan of the Tahirid dynasty, he sought out many such building projects during his reign.

The dome of Al-Bakiriyya Mosque has two main parts: an open courtyard called the Sanctuary or Pylon, and a covered prayer hall known as the House of Prayer. Several smaller domed extensions surround this main prayer hall.
Shibam's tall mudbrick towers were built to protect residents from Bedouin attacks. Each floor of these houses held only one or two rooms.
A tomb was added to the Al-Mahdi Mosque in Sanaa after the death of Imam Mahdi Abbas in 1768. This came more than a century after the mosque itself had been built in 1651.

In 1517, Wahhab was killed in battle by invading forces from the Mamluk Sultanate, who decapitated him and displayed his head on a pike in Sanaa. With the Tahirids defeated, the Mamluks ceded the former kingdom's territories, including Radda, to their allies in Yemen, the Zaydi imamate. The Zaydis, enemies of the Shafi'i-Sunni Tahirids, viewed the Amiriya Madrasa's opulence as a distraction from prayers and incompatible with their interpretation of Islam, and the Madrasa was left abandoned for several centuries as it fell into decay.

Yemeni folklore says Wahhab sometimes had every window of the Amiriya Madrasa filled with lanterns while he rode through the hills of Radda with his daughter. The story reflects the grandeur the Tahirid ruler brought to his project.

war.text: In 1517 Selim I acquired Medina and Mecca, and over the 16th century the Ottomans added the Hejaz and Asir regions along the Red Sea and the al-Hasa region on the Persian Gulf coast. These were the most populous parts of what was to become Saudi Arabia.
Migrin ibn Zamil, who inherited Al-Aḥsā, Qatif and Bahrain, fell in battle in Bahrain in 1521. He had failed to repel a Portuguese invasion of the island.
The Ottomans lost control of the al-Hasa region on the Persian Gulf coast to Arab tribes in the 17th century. They did not regain it until the 19th century.

The Al-Muntafiq tribe took over eastern Arabia and came under Ottoman suzerainty, but the Bani Khalid tribe revolted against them in the 17th century and took control. At its height their rule extended from Iraq to Oman, and they too came under Ottoman suzerainty.

Ottoman control of Arabian lands varied over four centuries with the strength of the empire's central authority. In the Hejaz the Sharifs of Mecca were largely left in control, though there was often an Ottoman governor and garrison in Mecca, while the interior stayed under petty tribal rulers.

The Bani Khalid remained staunch enemies of the Saudis and tried to invade Najd and Diriyyah to stop Saudi expansion, but failed. After conquering Najd, the Saudis invaded the Bani Khalid domain in Al-Aḥsā and deposed Al-'Ura'yir in 1793.

The Jabrids took control of eastern Arabia after overthrowing the Jarwanid dynasty in the 15th century. They clashed with Hormuz for more than two decades over the region's economic revenues, until finally agreeing to pay tribute in 1507.

literature.text: Nabati poetry, also known as Bedouin poetry or the people's poetry, arose in the 16th century as the Arabic dialect spread into Bedouin speech in the Arabian desert. Composed in colloquial Arabic rather than the strict classical rules of literary Arabic, it offered listeners an intimate window into Bedouin life, values and traditions.

Bedouin poets writing Nabati verse composed poems similar in structure, theme, metre and rhyme to the qasida of pre-Islamic poets such as Imru' al-Qais, whose works had set the classical standard for hundreds of years. Verse by illiterate Bedouin masters stayed close in spirit and language to these ancient models.

Many Nabati poets were nomadic Bedouins who lacked opportunities for formal education, so they never learned the classical Arabic structures used in literary poetry and did not apply them to their own verse. Their nomadic lifestyle, built around animals for transport and livelihood, shaped the poems and made them hard for sedentary scholars to interpret.

Ibn Daher, a prominent Nabati poet, lived in Ras Al Khaimah in the 16th century, and his work still influences the genre's poetry today. He was among the Bedouin poets whose verse helped establish Nabati as a distinct oral tradition of the Arabian Peninsula.

Ibn Li'bun, born in 1790 on the eastern coast of the Arabian Peninsula, became known as the Prince of the Nabati Poets. He corresponded with other poets across the region, and his verses later gave rise to many traditional popular tunes in Arabia.

politics.text: After the Ottomans conquered Mamluk territory in 1517, the whole Arabian peninsula came under the influence of Sultan Selim I. In the Hijaz, the sultan's role was first and foremost to take care of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He also had to provide safe passage for the many Muslims who traveled there to perform the Hajj.

Al-Mansur al-Qasim was a religious teacher at the Dawud mosque in Sana'a when one of his pupils urged him to claim the Zaydi imamate, an offer he first declined. Growing Ottoman suspicion eventually forced him to flee, and in September 1597 he formally set forth his claim to the imamate in Hajur.

In 1517 the Ottomans conquered Mamluk territory, and Selim I's acquisition of Mecca and Medina brought the whole Arabian peninsula under the sultan's influence. The Ottomans added the Hejaz, Asir and al-Hasa to their empire and claimed the interior too, though that claim stayed largely nominal.

In 1744 Muhammad ibn Saud, the tribal ruler of Ad-Dir'iyyah near Riyadh, joined forces with the religious leader Muhammad ibn Abd-al-Wahhab, founder of the Wahhabi movement. This alliance gave the ideological push for Saudi expansion and remains the basis of Saudi dynastic rule today.

The Ottoman sultan was sometimes called the "Servant of the Holy Places". Since Ottoman rulers could not claim lineage from the Prophet Muhammad, it was important to maintain an image of power and piety. They did this through construction projects, financial support and caretaking of Mecca and Medina.

By 1617 al-Mansur al-Qasim's forces had captured the important city of Sa'dah, and a truce concluded two years later confirmed his control over the entire area between Sana'a and Sa'dah. The city of Sana'a itself remained in Ottoman hands until his death in 1620.

The Ottoman sultan's role in the Hijaz was first to care for the holy cities of Mecca and Medina and to guarantee safe passage for Hajj pilgrims. Since Ottoman rulers could not claim descent from the Prophet Muhammad, they kept up an image of power and piety through construction, financial support and caretaking.

The main reason for the Ottoman push into Arabia in the 16th century was to thwart Portuguese attempts to attack the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. Controlling the Hejaz was therefore a defensive priority for the empire.

The first Saudi state, founded in 1744 around Riyadh, expanded rapidly. Control over southern and central Najd was complete by 1773, northern Najd was added in the late 1780s, and al-Hasa fell in 1792. Taif was taken in 1802 and Medina in 1804.

In the Hejaz, the Sharifs of Mecca were largely left in control of their territory, although there was often an Ottoman governor and garrison in Mecca. Meanwhile the interior stayed under a large number of petty tribal rulers, much as in previous centuries.

The Bani Khalid dominated the deserts around the Al-Ahsa and Al-Qatif oases in the 16th and 17th centuries. Under Barrak ibn Ghurayr of the Humaid clan they expelled Ottoman forces from the cities and towns in 1670 and proclaimed their own rule over the region.

When the emir of Uyayna adopted the ideas of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, the Khalidi chief ordered him to stop supporting Ibn Abd al-Wahhab and expel him. The emir agreed, and Ibn Abd al-Wahhab moved to neighboring Dir'iyyah, where he joined forces with the Al Saud.

In 1553, Ottoman orders were issued telling the Sharifs of Mecca to place the Najd region under their protection. Attacks by some tribes on the Hajj caravans may have been among the reasons that prompted the Sharif to raise complaints.

From 1578 the Sharifs of Mecca sent forays into the desert to conquer and punish the Najdi tribes that raided oases and tribes in the Hejaz. In 1578 the Sharifs' invasion involved 50,000 warriors, who reached Riyadh and sacked it, appointed a new ruler and imprisoned several influential citizens. The prisoners were released after a year in exchange for an agreement to pay an annual tribute. During the seventeenth century the Sharifs invaded Najd five times, in 1606, 1647, 1669, 1676 and 1697.

The Ottomans were forced out of Al-Hasa in 1680, yet they went on claiming it as part of the empire even though they held no sovereignty over the emirate. Their claim to the whole peninsula persisted through the seventeenth century, even where local rulers and tribal loyalists governed.

Ajwad ibn Zamil, who died in 1507, was the most prominent ruler of the Jabrids, who at their height controlled the whole Persian Gulf coast of Arabia, including Bahrain. After his death the kingdom was divided among his descendants. Migrin ibn Zamil inherited Al-Ahsa, Qatif and Bahrain, and fell in battle in 1521 trying to repel a Portuguese invasion of Bahrain.
Nasir bin Muhammad, an emir of Diriyah, was killed in 1672 (1084 AH). After his killing, Muhammad bin Muqrin assumed the Emirate of Diriyah for the second time.

In 1553 the Ottomans, through their emir in Al-Ahsa, appointed Sa'dun ibn Hamid as emir over parts of Al-Aridh and Najd, including Al-Uyaynah and Huraymila. That same year Ottoman orders told the Sharifs to place Najd among the territories under their protection, perhaps because tribes had attacked Hajj caravans.

Barrak ibn Ghurayr of the Bani Khalid made his capital at Al-Mubarraz, where remnants of his castle stand today. Arabian folklore also tells of a Bani Khalid chief who banned bedouin from poaching the eggs of the desert bustard, earning the tribe the name "protectors of the eggs of the habari".

After the death of Saud I in 1726, the oldest man in the family, Zaid bin Markhan bin Watban, succeeded him but was killed in 1726. Muhammad bin Saud then assumed the emirate of Diriyah and later became the first emir and imam of the first Saudi state.

philosophy.text: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703-1792) was an Arab Muslim scholar born in Najd who called for a return directly to the Quran and Hadith rather than relying on traditional interpretations. He opposed blind taqlid and insisted that every Muslim, male and female, personally read and study the Quran.

Ibn Abd al-Wahhab condemned the veneration of shrines and tombs of Muslim saints as heretical religious innovation, even idolatry. He is considered the eponymous founder of the Wahhabi movement, which took shape in Najd, his home region of the Arabian Peninsula.

The theologian Ibrahim al-Kurani migrated to Medina in 1652, where he remained for the rest of his life. There he became a disciple of Ahmad al-Qushashi, who initiated him into the Shattari Sufi order and gave him his daughter in marriage, and al-Kurani went on to serve as an imam at the Prophet's Mosque.

In 1744, Muhammad ibn Saud took in a religious scholar named Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, who came from the town of Al-Uyaynah, and agreed to implement his religious views. This alliance gave birth to the First Saudi State, with its capital at Diriyah.

Wahhabism began as a revivalist movement in the Arabian Peninsula in the early 18th century, whose adherents called themselves Muwahhidun, or Unitarians. Inspired by the medieval Hanbali scholar Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Abd al-Wahhab denounced Sufi practices as idolatrous innovations and called for the use of ijtihad.

Al-Kurani was once a proponent of the mystical doctrine of Wahdat al-Wujud before later adhering to Atharism. In 1682 he wrote a treatise defending Ibn Arabi's theology of Wahdat al-Wujud, refuting claims that it was anthropomorphist, pantheist or corporealist.

The Rassid Zaydi dynasty was re-established in Yemen under Al-Mansur al-Qasim following an Ottoman invasion in the 16th century. Zaydi philosophy prized rationalism over Quranic literalism and rejected the practice of religious dissimulation known as taqiyya.

The 1744 pact between Ibn Abd al-Wahhab and Muhammad ibn Saud became a mutual support arrangement between their descendants, the Al ash-Sheikh and the Al Saud. The Al Saud upheld the Al ash-Sheikh's religious authority and propagated Wahhabi doctrine, while the Al ash-Sheikh's moral authority helped legitimize Al Saud political rule.

culture.text: Bi'r al-Azab, a suburb built between Sanaa's city walls and the new Jewish Quarter, was first mentioned in historical sources in 1627. It was known for its many gardens and was originally called the Turkish Quarter.

Many attitudes and traditions in Saudi Arabia are about 300 years old by 2027. They are derived from Arab civilization and Islamic heritage. The society is described as religious, conservative, traditional and family-oriented.

In Eastern Arabia, children dress in traditional attire and go door-to-door singing traditional songs to receive sweets from neighbours. This celebration, called Gargee'an, takes place on the 15th night of Sha'ban and again on the 15th night of Ramadan. The tradition has existed for hundreds of years.

The Wahhabi movement arose in the 18th century and now predominates in Saudi Arabia. Following the principle of "enjoining good and forbidding wrong", many limitations and prohibitions on behavior and dress are enforced there, both legally and socially.

According to Arabian folklore, one chief of the Bani Khalid tried to protect the prized desert bustard, the habari, from extinction. He forbade the bedouin in his realm from poaching its eggs. The tribe, which dominated the deserts around Al-Ahsa and Qatif in the 16th and 17th centuries, was nicknamed "protectors of the eggs of the habari".

Gargee'an, the Gulf tradition of children collecting sweets door-to-door, looks superficially like Halloween trick-or-treating. However, it has no known common origins with Halloween, nor does it share its macabre characteristics.
